issues.description: The UML in the problem statement specifies numberOfTutors as type int, but the solution declares the attribute as type short. This discrepancy can confuse students about the expected type for the attribute and may lead to mismatches with tests or the expected constructor/setter signatures.
issues.suggestedFix: Use int for numberOfTutors consistently. Update the solution's field declaration from short to int, and ensure the template and any constructors/getters/setters use int as well to match the UML and expected tests.

issues.description: The problem statement and UML imply the constructor should accept numberOfTutors as an int (matching the UML attribute type), but the solution's constructor signature declares the last parameter as short. This difference creates a mismatch students may not anticipate when implementing the constructor or when tests expect an int parameter.
issues.suggestedFix: Change the constructor parameter type for numberOfTutors in the solution to int (and update the template accordingly) so the constructor signature matches the UML and expected usage: Lecture(String lectureName, int numberOfInscribedStudents, int numberOfGuestStudents, int numberOfLecturers, int numberOfTutors).

issues.description: The setter for numberOfTutors in the solution uses a short parameter (setNumberOfTutors(short)), while the UML in the problem statement indicates numberOfTutors is an int. Tests and students will expect a setter that accepts an int, causing a parameter type mismatch.
issues.suggestedFix: Update the setter signature to accept an int (public void setNumberOfTutors(int numberOfTutors)) and adjust the internal field type to int. Ensure getter/setter types are consistent with the UML and constructor signature.
